notes.decision: Translated 'Concerning the Two Substances.' ⲧⲟⲩⲥⲓⲁ takes the feminine article on the Greek loanword ⲟⲩⲥⲓⲁ; ⲥⲛⲧⲉ = 'two' (fem.). The chapter title is flanked by the chapter number ⲣⲕ̄ (120) on both sides, a standard Kephalaia heading-bracket convention.

Translated 'our Father examined.' ⲙⲟⲩⲥ = Lyc. variant of ⲙⲟⲩⲍ/ⲙⲟⲩϣⲧ̄ 'examine, scrutinize' (cf. ⲙⲟⲩⲍ in accumulated vocabulary), here with ⲥ for ⲍ. The dialogue-frame opens with the Apostle's examination of his disciples or audience.

Translated 'Two substances are those existing from the beginning' — the foundational Manichaean dualist proposition opening this kephalaion. ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲣⲭⲏ = 'from the beginning' (Greek ἀρχή with directional ⲛ̄-).
Translated 'every thing.' ⲥⲱⲃ = Lyc. ϩⲱⲃ 'thing, work' (with ⲥ for ϩ — unusual but consistent with this manuscript's occasional ⲥ/ⲍ alternation for standard Coptic ϩ).

Translated 'one substance which exists.' This is the opponents' monistic position that Mani is refuting: a single ⲟⲩⲥⲓⲁ from which all things including evil must derive. The polemic targets a position that would make God responsible for evil by denying any reality outside Him.

Read ⲡⲟ̄ⲁⲗ as 'the lie' (Lyc. variant of ϭⲟⲗ 'lie/falsehood'); ⲧⲙⲛⲧⲙⲛⲧⲣⲉ ⲛⲛⲟⲩⲭ as 'the false witness of falsehood' — biblical-legal pair (cf. Ten Commandments). Note ⲡⲟ̄ⲁⲗ is distinct from glossary ⲡⲁ̄ⲗⲁⲍ 'strife'; here vice-catalogue context disambiguates as 'lie.'
Greek καταλαλιά + κατηγορία rendered 'slander of accusation' — the slanderous speech-act that constitutes legal accusation. Both retained as Greek-derived sin-terms.

ⲡⲍⲁⲩⲣⲉ tentatively rendered 'sorcery' — possibly Lyc. for ϩⲁⲣⲉ/ϩⲣⲉ in magical-cursing register; positioned in the catalogue immediately after ⲙⲁⲅⲓⲁ 'magic.' Confidence moderate. ⲧⲥⲉⲧⲉ ⲛ̄ⲣⲉϩⲟⲩⲱⲙ literally 'the fire of one-who-eats' = the consuming/devouring fire, an image of destructive passion or possibly the punitive fire of judgment.

ⲃⲗⲁⲗⲉ taken as Lyc. reflex of ⲃⲗ̄ⲗⲉ 'be blind' — 'in which a man is blinded' (the desire of fornication blinds him). Alternative reading 'is loosed/let-loose' (from ⲃⲱⲗ family) is also possible but less idiomatic. Translated 'is blinded.'

ⲡⲉϥⲧⲏⲩ literally 'his wind/breath/spirit'; in moral-anthropological context = his impulse, his agitating breath of desire. ⲉⲙⲁϩⲍⲣⲁⲕ = Lyc. negative habitual 'not at rest' (ⲍⲣⲁⲕ from ϩⲣⲟⲕ 'still'). Captures the restless agitation of desire never satisfied.

Privative ⲙⲛⲧⲁⲧ-ⲥⲓ 'state-of-not-being-filled/satisfied' = insatiability; ⲡⲙⲁⲙⲟⲛⲁⲥ = Aramaic loan via Greek μαμωνᾶς (cf. Matt 6:24). Captures the unquenchable greed identified with material wealth as cosmic principle.
Lyc. negative habitual 'not being satisfied/filled' + ⲡⲉϥⲁⲍⲉ 'his lifespan' (in glossary as ⲡⲁⲍⲉ). The greedy man is never satisfied throughout his entire lifespan.
ⲡⲛⲁ̄ = standard Coptic abbreviation of πνεῦμα 'spirit'; ⲉⲧⲍⲁⲩ qualitative 'evil' (Lyc. for ⲉⲧϩⲟⲟⲩ). 'The evil spirit' as cosmic principle whose works manifest as the listed sins.

ⲛⲁⲭⲟⲩ from ⲛⲟⲩϫⲉ 'cast/throw' with 3pl object. The rhetorical question 'who has cast them into the heart of men?' is the polemical pivot — if not a power outside God, then God is implicated; the absurdity exposes the opponents' position.

ⲟⲩⲱϣϥ̄ = 'destroy, shatter, break.' The voice here is that of the personified evils (or perhaps God's adversary's perspective): 'why are you destroying me?' — the rhetorical move dramatizes the dilemma posed to the opponents.

ⲛⲱϩ = Lyc. 'mine' (= Sah. ⲛⲟⲩⲓ̈). 'If they are mine' — the conditional addresses ownership/responsibility for the evils. The argument: if God owns the evils, they cannot be condemned in those who do them.

notes.decision: Reading the line-23 restoration [ⲧⲉ] as completing ⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉ 'has not' (idiomatic 'X has no Y therein'). The argument: 'For if God established them alone, then the one who does them has no sin therein' — the reductio that follows from the opponents' position.
ⲭⲓⲟ̄ⲁⲗ from ϫⲓ-ⲟⲩⲁ 'utter blasphemy' (Lyc. ⲭ for ϫ). The accusation: by denying any reality outside God you are the very ones who blaspheme against Him, since you make Him source of evil.
ⲟⲩⲍⲉⲡⲧ = Lyc. for ⲟⲩⲥⲱⲡⲧ̄/ⲍⲉⲡⲧ 'rebuke, sharp judgment' (cf. glossary ⲟⲩⲍⲡⲧⲉ 'rebuke/sternness'). The Manichaean teacher pronounces a verdict against the monists.
Greek πονηρός 'the Evil One' — capitalized as cosmic-personal designation of the principle of evil, the dualistic counter-pole to God. The closing identification names what the monists deny exists.

The transcription symbol ⳨ functions consistently as the letter ⲧ in this manuscript: ⲛ̄⳨ⲍⲉ = ⲛ̄ⲧⲍⲉ 'thus' (glossary), ⲡⲓ⳨ⲟⲩ = ⲡⲓⲧⲟⲩ 'the five' (l.7), ⳨ⲛⲉⲩ = ⲧⲛⲉⲩ 'behold' (l.27). Rendered as ⲧ throughout.

Translated 'sweet' as antithesis to ⲉⲧⲥⲁϣⲉ 'bitter' in line 2 — the page's structuring gustatory-correspondential dyad (bitter trees vs. sweet fruits). The form is irregular; possible alternative readings include 'chosen' (ⲉⲧⲥⲁⲧⲡ̄) or a Lycopolitan reflex of ⲉⲧϩⲗⲟϭ. Confidence moderate.

Preserved untranslated/transliterated; the form is obscure. Possibly Lycopolitan reflex of ⲧⲱⲃⲉ 'seal' (cf. accumulated ⲡⲧⲁⲃⲉϩ 'imprint/seal') with possessive nuance, or a verbal form. Glossed tentatively as 'he sealed.' Confidence low.

ⲛ̄ⲧⲁϩ is the Lycopolitan emphatic intensive 'himself' (cf. line 11 ⲛ̄ⲧⲁϩ 'himself'). The preceding ⲣⲁϩ is part of the lost word/phrase referring to the subject (likely the Father or his name); rendered 'himself' as completing the intensive construction.

Read as Lycopolitan plural of ⲛⲟⲩⲭ/ⲡⲟⲁⲗ 'lie, falsehood' = 'lies' (cf. accumulated ⲡⲟⲁⲗ 'the lie'). The line 'all the wickednesses are lies which came to be from him' echoes the polemical critique that the Errant doctrine treats wickedness as having divine origin.

Direct correspondential register: 'separating the Beautiful one (= the Light/God) forth from the Darkness' — capitalized as cosmic principle per terminology guide. Standard Manichaean cosmogonic act of separation.

ⲡⲙⲏⲧ here = ⲡⲙⲛⲧⲣⲉ 'the witness/testimony' rather than 'the midst.' The 'witness of the Judge of Truth' (cf. accumulated ⲡⲕⲣⲓⲧⲏⲥ ⲛⲧⲉ ⲧⲙⲏⲉ) is the standard Manichaean eschatological warrant. The chapter closes by appealing to this judicial witness as the guarantee that the disciples shall see at death what the Apostle has declared.
